summary: Suggests a change in how FTP client programs behave, so FTP works better through firewalls. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Some doors let people in only one way. This memo suggests a change in how file-fetching programs knock so firewalls stay happy.

questions: why does ftp not work through firewalls
what is the ftp pasv command
subtitle: Why FTP clients should use PASV so that data connections pass through packet-filter firewalls.

tldr.problem: FTP normally has the server open the data connection back to the client, which looks like an incoming call to an unknown port and does not work well with packet filter firewalls.
tldr.mechanism: Clients send the PASV command, so the server opens a passive port and the client makes an outgoing connection to it.
tldr.outcome: No protocol change is needed, and vendors are urged to switch FTP clients from PORT to PASV. An optional APSV command is outlined.

today: RFC 1579 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata records no obsoleting or updating RFC. It describes a suggested change to client behavior rather than a new protocol.

sections.title: The Firewall Problem
sections.content:
FTP uses a secondary TCP connection to transmit files. By default the FTP server makes an active open to the FTP client. Packet filter based firewalls, in general, cannot permit incoming calls to random port numbers.

By the specification, the server opens the data connection from its port 20 to the same port on the client as was used for the control connection. Most clients do not behave that way. They use a new connection for each transfer, pick a new port each time to avoid TCP's TIMEWAIT state, and announce it with a PORT command.

Neither scenario is firewall-friendly. Blocking only port numbers below 1024 is risky, because dangerous services such as X Windows live at higher numbers.
sections.eli5: The guard blocks strangers knocking on random doors, but the old way of fetching files made the server knock on a random door of the client.

sections.title: How PASV Helps
sections.content:
Outgoing calls cause fewer problems. A TCP packet with the ACK bit set cannot be the one that starts a connection, so filters can pass such packets in the outbound direction only.

The needed mechanism already exists. When the client sends PASV, the server does a passive TCP open on some random port and tells the client the port number. The client then performs the active open. A server that does not understand PASV returns 500 Command not understood, and the client can fall back to current behavior.
sections.eli5: Instead of the server calling the client, the client calls the server. The server says which door to use, and the guard lets the client's outgoing call pass.

sections.title: Recommendation and Optional APSV
sections.content:
The memo recommends that vendors convert FTP clients, including FTP proxy agents such as Gopher daemons, to use PASV instead of PORT. There is no reason not to use it even for non-firewall transfers. Because the format of the PASV response is not well defined, clients and servers should follow the recommendations of RFC 1123.

PASV adds no extra messages for most current clients. As a possible enhancement, the client could send a new command APSV ("all passive") at startup, and the server would answer transfer requests with a new reply code 151 containing the port to use. The memo says APSV had not been implemented.
sections.eli5: The memo asks everyone to use the client-calls-server way. It also dreams up a shortcut that says it once at the start, but nobody had built that yet.

sections.title: Security Trade-offs
sections.content:
The memo admits that packet filters are hard to configure and that some people object to permitting arbitrary outgoing calls. Using PASV can improve the security of gateway machines, which no longer need to create ports that an outsider might connect to first.

The server side now has to accept calls to random ports. The author argues this is manageable because there are many fewer FTP servers than clients: filters can allow access to just a few machines, and servers can use only very high-numbered ports for data.
sections.eli5: The problem moves to the server's door, but there are far fewer servers than clients, so guarding them is easier.
